endorsements.quote: Translating twin-guided de-escalation into clinical practice will require a prospective, adequately powered randomized trial in which twin-derived risk stratification is prespecified as an enrollment criterion rather than applied retrospectively.

The road ahead requires a concerted interdisciplinary effort to build the infrastructure, prospectively validate the algorithms across institutions, and establish governance frameworks for AI-assisted decisions, with an immediate priority of designing multicenter feasibility trials that test individual twin components against standard of care in head-to-head comparisons.

It is essential to recognize, however, that high predictive performance on internal validation datasets does not, by itself, confer clinical trustworthiness; prospective external validation, transparent reporting of model limitations, and robust governance frameworks for AI-assisted decisions are prerequisites for responsible integration.

unlisted_practices: Establish an independent data safety monitoring board for trials of twin-guided de-escalation to detect interim safety signals arising from twin-prediction errors.
Engage regulators early, for example through an FDA presubmission meeting, for trials using algorithmic risk stratification as an enrollment criterion.
Apply feature harmonization methods such as ComBat to correct vendor- and reconstruction-dependent variation in radiomic features before cross-modal model fusion.
Use multirate alignment approaches such as hierarchical Bayesian models or multirate Kalman filtering to reconcile mismatched temporal resolutions across data streams.
Develop hybrid models that combine radiomics with mechanistic biological constraints.
Treat synthetic control arms as supplementary, hypothesis-generating evidence rather than a substitute for randomized concurrent controls.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint proposing a conceptual framework and technical roadmap for digital twins in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, discussing opportunities, challenges, and implementation barriers rather than reporting an empirical study.
